intro: This unit reads two famous passages up close. The first is Bava Metzia 59b, the story of the oven of Akhnai. A rabbi calls on miracles and a voice from heaven, and the majority still rules against him. The second is Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Makkot 7a, where the rabbis teach that one life is a whole world and argue about whether a court should ever put anyone to death.

Both passages show the course's two threads. Argument: you will trace how each sugya moves through question, proof, objection and answer. Mercy: you will see whom each ruling protects, from the teacher who lost a vote to the person on trial. You will read verses in the public-domain JPS 1917 translation and rabbinic passages in careful paraphrase.

By the end you will be able to cite a passage by tractate and page, explain what it says, and describe how Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers have read it. This course describes those readings. It does not tell you which one is right.
bigQuestion: How does the Talmud balance the authority of the law with mercy for the person the law affects?

test.q: In which tractate is the oven of Akhnai story found?
What theme frames the oven story?
test.why: The story sits inside Bava Metzia's chapter on ona'ah.

test.q: Which rabbi quoted 'It is not in heaven'?
test.why: Rabbi Joshua answered the heavenly voice.

test.q: Which verse does Rabbi Jeremiah read as 'incline after the majority'?
What did Elijah report God said?
Who dressed in black to tell Rabbi Eliezer of the ban?
test.why: Akiva chose to deliver the news gently.

test.q: According to Imma Shalom, which gates are never locked?
Which Mishnah says one life is like a whole world?
Why, in Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, was one person created?
choices: To set the price of goods
To teach the worth of each single life

test.q: How many judges did the Mishnah require for capital cases?
In capital cases, how does the court open?
choices: With a vote of the eldest

test.q: What did Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say?
choices: Had we sat on the court, no one would have been executed

test.q: Who replied that they would multiply murderers?
Which statement fits how the Talmud treats minority views?
choices: It records them by name even when they lose
It erases them after a vote
test.why: Rabbi Eliezer's and Akiva's minority views survive.

test.q: Which translation of the Bible is public domain and quoted in this unit?
test.why: The JPS Tanakh of 1917 is public domain.

write.prompt: Does the Talmud care more about settling the law or about protecting the person the law affects? Cite Bava Metzia 59b, Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Mishnah Makkot 1:10. Explain what each says and how different readers have read it.
tips: Name each text by tractate and page or chapter and mishnah.
Attribute every view to the rabbi or reader who holds it.
Give the minority view its strongest form.
Compare readings rather than judging them.
Use unit terms such as ona'ah, sugya and aggadah.
